questions.stem: Which of the following correctly distinguishes recruitment from selection?
options: Recruitment attracts applicants; selection chooses between them
Recruitment chooses the candidate; selection advertises the role
They are two words for the same process
Recruitment is internal; selection is external
questions.why: Recruitment is about generating a pool of suitable applicants. Selection is the process of choosing from that pool through interviews, tests and references.
whyNot: This reverses the two.
They are distinct stages and examiners test the distinction.
Both internal and external recruitment are followed by a selection stage.

questions.stem: Which term is defined as: training given to a new employee when they join, covering the business, the role and its procedures?
options: Induction training
On-the-job training
Off-the-job training
Job enrichment
questions.why: Induction is short, cheap and has the clearest return: it reduces early mistakes and early leavers. Skipping it is a false economy.
whyNot: On-the-job training happens while doing the job, usually alongside a colleague, and continues beyond joining.
Off-the-job training happens away from the workplace, such as a course.
Job enrichment is a motivation method, not a type of training.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an advantage of internal recruitment?
options: It is cheaper and faster, and the candidate already knows the business
It brings fresh ideas from outside the business
It gives access to skills the business does not currently have
It avoids creating any further vacancy
questions.why: No advertising or agency fees, no long notice period, and the person's work is already known, so the risk is lower.
whyNot: New ideas are the advantage of EXTERNAL recruitment. Internal reproduces the existing culture.
Also external. If the skill is not in the business, internal recruitment cannot find it.
Internal promotion creates a vacancy at the level below, which is one of its drawbacks.

questions.stem: What is the main drawback of on-the-job training?
options: The trainer stops producing while training, and bad habits can be passed on
It is the most expensive form of training
It teaches skills irrelevant to the business
It requires the employee to leave the workplace
questions.why: It is cheap and relevant, but an experienced colleague is diverted from their own work, and whatever they do wrong gets taught to the next person too.
whyNot: It is normally the cheapest form of training. Off-the-job is the expensive one.
It teaches exactly what the business does, which is both its strength and its limitation.
That describes off-the-job training.

questions.stem: Why can investing in training increase the risk of losing an employee?
options: Training makes them more qualified and therefore more attractive to competitors
Trained employees are legally free to leave immediately
Training always reduces job satisfaction
Trained employees must be made redundant
questions.why: A recognised qualification is portable. The counter is that good training is itself a reason to stay, so the answer is to pair training with pay and progression rather than to avoid training.
whyNot: Notice periods apply regardless of training.
Training normally raises satisfaction, because development is a Herzberg motivator.
There is no such link.

questions.stem: A business needs a specialist skill that takes years to qualify in and that nobody internally has. What should it do?
options: Recruit externally, because the skill cannot be created internally in the time available
Promote internally and hope for the best
Use induction training to create the qualification
Outsource its entire operation
questions.why: Internal recruitment can only redeploy skills the business already holds. Where a qualification takes years, external recruitment is the only realistic route.
whyNot: Promoting someone without the qualification does not produce the skill and risks the work being done badly.
Induction covers the business and the role, not a multi-year professional qualification.
A disproportionate response to a single vacancy.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best definition of labour turnover?
options: The proportion of a workforce that leaves over a period of time
The total wage bill for a period
The revenue generated per employee
The number of employees a business has
questions.why: Turnover measures how many leave. It matters financially because every leaver restarts the full recruitment, induction and training cost cycle.
whyNot: That is the wage bill or labour cost.
That is labour productivity measured by revenue.
That is headcount.

questions.stem: Why is induction training usually considered the training with the clearest return?
options: It is cheap and short, and it reduces early mistakes and early leavers
It produces a recognised professional qualification
It replaces the need for all other training
It is required by law in all countries
questions.why: Most people who leave within the first month do so because they were left to work things out alone. A short, cheap induction prevents a very expensive outcome.
whyNot: Qualifications come from off-the-job training.
It is the beginning of training, not a substitute for the rest.
Health and safety elements are often required, but the full induction is not universally mandated.

questions.stem: A remote island resort finds off-the-job training unusually expensive. Why, and what follows?
options: Staff must travel to reach providers, so most training is done on-the-job and through multi-skilling
Off-the-job training is banned on islands
Remote businesses need no training
On-the-job training costs more in remote locations
questions.why: Travel and accommodation are added to the course fee, and the employee is absent for longer. The practical response is to train internally and multi-skill, which also makes retention more valuable because replacements are hard to start quickly.
whyNot: There is no such restriction. It is a cost and logistics problem.
Remote operations need training at least as much, because help is further away.
On-the-job training is unaffected by location; it happens where the work is.

questions.stem: Which calculation best supports an argument for investing in retention rather than recruitment?
options: Comparing the cost of replacing an employee with the cost of keeping them
Comparing the wage bill with total revenue
Calculating the market share of the business
Calculating the gross profit margin
questions.why: Recruitment fees, management time, induction, training and the vacancy period add up to a replacement cost. Setting that against a pay rise or a training budget turns a general argument into a quantified one, which is where the application and evaluation marks are.
whyNot: A useful ratio, but it says nothing about the cost of turnover.
Market share is unrelated to staffing decisions.
A profitability measure, not a staffing comparison.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a drawback of external recruitment?
options: It can demotivate existing staff who were passed over
It reproduces the existing culture with no new ideas
It creates a vacancy at the level below
The candidate already knows the business too well
questions.why: If staff see an outsider appointed to a role they hoped for, the signal is that there is no path upwards, and some of them will leave.
whyNot: That is a drawback of internal recruitment.
Also internal: promoting someone leaves their old role empty.
An external candidate does not know the business, which is a drawback in the other direction.
